div.p: In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tooluse errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce τ -Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agentuser-environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to τ -Bench and τ -Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, τ -Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision. div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Large language models have rapidly evolved into agents capable of planning (Zhu et al., 2025), calling external tools, maintaining long-term memory (Uddin et al., 2026), and completing longhorizon tasks in interactive environments (Wang et al., 2024). Recent benchmarks have made these evaluations increasingly realistic by introducing complex tool dependencies, stateful environments, and multi-turn user interactions (Yao et al., 2024;He et al., 2025b;Yu et al., 2026b;Barres et al., 2025). In parallel, recent agent-training methods generate large collections of successful trajectories from executable environments (Li et al., 2025;Liu et al., 2026;Saeidi et al., 2026a;Wang et al., 2026;Xu et al., 2026b). However, both evaluation and data generation still largely rely on terminal task success as the main signal of agent quality (Saeidi et al., 2026c). A trajectory may eventually solve the task while repeatedly asking unnecessary questions, requesting information that could be obtained through tools, or relying excessively on the user instead of interacting with the environment (Mishra et al., 2025). Such trajectories receive positive task reward despite exhibiting undesirable behavior for user-facing agents. This exposes an important limitation of current agent harnesses, which measure whether the task is completed but provide little signal about whether the interaction itself is efficient.

We introduce τ -Emotion-Bench and Tracer to address this gap through an emotion-conditioned agent-user-environment harness. τ -Emotion-Bench contains 580 executable tasks across ten domains and systematically varies user behavior through five emotion families and fine-grained behavioral attributes while preserving the underlying task objective. Tracer constructs these tasks through grounded, policy-valid tool workflows and uses the same harness to generate training trajectories (See Figure 2). The key difference from conventional trajectory collection is that the user simulator contributes an additional interaction-aware reward signal. When an agent repeatedly asks unnecessary questions or fails to make sufficient progress, the user may become dissatisfied and terminate the interaction, preventing the trajectory from receiving a successful reward even if the task could eventually have been completed. Consequently, Tracer filters out successful but interaction-inefficient behavior and favors trajectories in which the agent asks only for information that is genuinely unavailable while relying more heavily on tools and the environment. This produces training data with a better balance between necessary user interaction and autonomous task execution.

Our experiments show that τ -Emotion-Bench remains challenging even for strong frontier models. With GLM-5.2 as the emotion-conditioned user simulator, the best evaluated model, GLM-5.3, reaches 78.6% Avg@3 but only 66.5% average Pass^3. Under Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as the user simulator, the strongest model, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, reaches 55.9% Avg@3 and only 32.2% average Pass^3. These results leave substantial room for improvement in reliable task completion across both evaluation settings. Importantly, the gains from Tracer supervision remain substantial across model scales. Under GLM-5.2, Tracer-High improves the corresponding Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models by 17. 1-25.2 percentage points in Avg@3, with Tracer-High-8B reaching 54.7%. Tracer-Low, trained on only 1,498 trajectories from four domains, generalizes to six unseen domains and achieves the strongest average Pass^3 among the compared agent-training methods at all three model scales. The learned behavior also transfers to τ -Bench (Yao et al., 2024) and τ -Trait (He et al., 2025a), which use different tasks and user simulators. Our behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and conversational follow-up, while policy violations and unnecessary interaction remain important failure modes. Together, these results show that emotion-conditioned interaction can serve not only as a stress test for agent reliability, but also as a useful reward signal for collecting more effective agent-training trajectories. Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

• τ -Emotion-Bench. We introduce a ten-domain benchmark and emotion-conditioned agentuser-environment harness for evaluating tool-calling agents under diverse user behaviors while preserving the underlying task objective. • Interaction-aware trajectory generation. We introduce a scalable pipeline for generating grounded agentic tasks and an interaction-aware reward signal that filters inefficient trajectories with excessive user dependence while favoring effective tool use. • Generalizable agent training. We show that Tracer consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales and transfers to unseen domains, external benchmarks, and different user simulators with a relatively small training set.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Interactive Tool-Use and User Simulation. Agent benchmarks have increasingly shifted from isolated function calls toward stateful interaction among agents, users, and executable environments. ToolTalk, ToolSandbox, and τ -Bench introduce conversational tool use, user simulation, and policyconstrained multi-turn interaction (Farn & Shin, 2023;Lu et al., 2025;Yao et al., 2024), while τ 2 -Bench, VitaBench, and WildToolBench further increase interaction complexity through shared environments, ambiguous requests, shifting intent, and conversational transitions (Barres et al., 2025;He et al., 2025b;Yu et al., 2026a). More recent work studies variation in user behavior, with τ -Trait controlling traits such as impatience and confusion and RealUserSim grounding user behavior in real conversational profiles (He et al., 2025a;Zhu et al., 2026a). Related affective benchmarks, including EIBench and TEA-Bench, focus on emotion management and emotional support (Zhu et al., 2026b;Sui et al., 2026). However, these works do not systematically measure how controlled emotional variation affects task-oriented tool use while preserving the same executable task and success conditions. As summarized in Table 1, τ -Emotion-Bench fills this gap by varying emotion and behavioral expression while keeping the underlying task and environment fixed.

div.head: Synthetic Environments and Agent
div.p: Training. A parallel line of work scales agent training through synthetic environments and executable trajectories. VULCAN constructs deterministic tool-use environments from API specifications and collects executable multi-step trajectories (Saeidi et al., 2026a), while EnvScaler, Agent World Model, and Simia generate stateful environments and training data for supervised and reinforcement learning (Song et al., 2026;Wang et al., 2026;Li et al., 2025). EigenData and SPADE further improve synthetic data generation through executable verification and adaptive environment construction (Gao et al., 2026;Liu et al., 2026). However, these methods primarily assess trajectories through task success, verification, or environment difficulty. In contrast, Tracer introduces an interaction-aware signal through the emotion-conditioned user harness, where unnecessary dependence on the user can lead to dissatisfaction and terminate the trajectory. Consequently, Tracer favors successful trajectories that balance necessary clarification with autonomous tool and environment interaction rather than task completion alone.

div.head: PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Following τ -Bench (Yao et al., 2024), we formulate each task as a partially observable Markov decision process (S, A, O, T, R, U ), where S is the state space, A is the agent action space, O is the observation space, T is the transition function, R is the task reward, and U is the space of user instructions. The agent interacts with both an executable environment and a simulated user. Accordingly, the action space contains tool calls and natural-language responses, while observations contain tool outputs and user messages.
τ -Emotion-Bench extends this interaction with an emotion condition e ∈ E. Given a task instruction u ∈ U and the interaction history h t , the user response at turn t is sampled according to

div.p: The task instruction, environment, and task objective remain unchanged across emotion conditions. The emotion condition is fixed within an episode, while its expression evolves with the interaction history. The simulator can therefore react differently to successful progress, repeated clarification, unnecessary requests, or other interaction behavior without changing the underlying task.

In addition to producing natural-language responses, the user can terminate the episode with either ###STOP### or ###UNSATISFIED###. The former indicates that the user considers the interaction complete, following the termination mechanism of τ -Bench, while the latter indicates that the accumulated interaction has become sufficiently unsatisfactory to continue. An episode therefore ends when the task interaction terminates normally, when the user becomes unsatisfied, or when the maximum interaction horizon is reached. If ###UNSATISFIED### is emitted before successful task completion, the trajectory receives -1 reward. This extension preserves the original task objective while allowing the interaction itself to affect whether a trajectory is considered successful.

div.head: TASK CONSTRUCTION
div.p: We construct grounded and executable tasks across ten tool-use domains, following the general interactive tool-use setup represented by τ -Bench, τ -Trait, and ToolOrchestra (Yao et al., 2024;He et al., 2025a;Su et al., 2025). Our construction separates the generation of valid tool workflows from their grounding in concrete environment states. For each domain, we construct a directed tool graph G = (V, E) following the dependency-based formulation of VULCAN (Saeidi et al., 2026a). Each node v ∈ V corresponds to a task-relevant tool, while an edge (v i , v j ) ∈ E indicates that v j can validly follow v i according to the tool interfaces and domain policy. Candidate edges are inferred from tool definitions, execution behavior, and policy constraints, and the graph is manually verified before task generation. We then sample valid paths from G to obtain workflows of varying complexity and compose multiple paths when constructing multi-intent tasks. Detailed sampling configurations are provided in Appendix A, with additional environment details in Appendix D.

A sampled workflow defines the sequence of operations needed to complete a task, but leaves the specific entities and arguments unspecified. The grounding agent fills in these details using the executable environment, producing a valid reference trajectory. The preference agent then turns the grounded task into a natural user request and adds preferences that are feasible without changing the task's intended outcome. Separately, the feeling generator uses the user context and requested actions to describe the user's likely emotional state. It does not access the environment database, so the generated description cannot rely on information that would be unavailable to the user.

div.head: EMOTION MODELING AND USER SIMULATION
div.p: We next map the task-specific feeling generated in Section 3.2 to a controlled emotion condition.

Our emotion space follows the Atlas of Emotions (Ekman, 2016) and contains five families with 22 fine-grained emotions. These are Anger (annoyance, frustration, argumentativeness, bitterness, exasperation), Fear (anxiety, nervousness, dread, desperation), Disgust (dislike, aversion, distaste, repugnance), Sadness (disappointment, discouragement, helplessness, hopelessness, sorrow), and Enjoyment (relief, pride, peace, excitement). We further combine each emotion with three behavioral dimensions covering politeness, urgency, and trust, yielding 594 conditions that capture both what the user feels and how that feeling is expressed. To map each free-form task feeling into this space, we use natural-language anchors and a multi-head classifier over the fine-grained emotion and behavioral attributes, then use semantic similarity to the anchors in the classifier's learned embedding space to select the final condition. The corresponding natural-language instruction is provided to the user simulator rather than the discrete labels. Further details of the taxonomy, anchor construction, and mapping procedure are provided in Appendix A.1.

Given the selected emotion instruction, the user simulator generates each response conditioned on the task and the evolving conversation history. Rather than enforcing a fixed surface style, the instruction acts as a behavioral constraint, allowing the same emotion condition to be expressed differently as the interaction develops. This provides controlled variation in user behavior without scripting individual turns. The same interaction mechanism is used during Tracer trajectory collection, where the simulator's responses provide an additional signal for selecting trajectories beyond environment-level task success. We verify generated tasks before including them in the benchmark. A task must specify a concrete objective, provide sufficient information for execution, admit an executable reference trajectory, and remain consistent with the corresponding domain policy. Reference trajectories are validated through deterministic replay, while model-based adjudication is used only when the deterministic outcome is inconclusive. All 580 evaluation tasks are additionally reviewed manually under the same criteria, and this process identifies 101 tasks requiring correction before inclusion. As an additional solvability check, a human tool-calling agent successfully completes selected tasks on which the evaluated models fail across all trials.

div.head: TASK VERIFICATION AND DATA COMPOSITION
div.p: The final benchmark contains 70 evaluation tasks from each of Airline, Retail, Telecom, and Telehealth and 50 from each of School, Basketball, Restaurant, Travel, Movie, and Bank. We additionally generate 1,958 training trajectories across the ten domains.

div.head: EXPERIMENTS
div.p: We evaluate τ -Emotion-Bench and Tracer through four questions. (Q1) How robust are frontier agents to emotion-conditioned users? (Q2) Can Tracer improve smaller agents and narrow the gap to frontier models? (Q3) Do Tracer-trained behaviors transfer to unseen tool-use domains with less training data? (Q4) Do these gains transfer to benchmarks with different tasks and user simulators? We first describe the evaluated models, training baselines, and evaluation protocol, followed by in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-benchmark results.

div.head: EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: Models. We evaluate a broad set of strong open-weight and proprietary LLM agents, covering both thinking and non-thinking configurations when available. Our evaluation includes Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025), Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 (Yang et al., 2025), Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (Xu et al., 2026a), Gemma-4-31B-it (Team, 2026), GLM-5.3 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Kimi-K2.7-Code (Team et al., 2025), MiniMax-M2.7, MiniMax-M3 (Chen et al., 2026) and Muse-Glimmer-30B (Meta Superintelligence Lab, 2026). To study whether Tracer-generated supervision can improve substantially smaller agents, we additionally fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B under two training settings.

Tracer-High is trained on 1,958 trajectories generated across all ten τ -Emotion-Bench domains, while Tracer-Low is trained on 1,498 trajectories from only Airline, Retail, Telecom, and Telehealth domains. This setup allows us to measure both the effectiveness of Tracer supervision and the extent to which the learned behavior transfers beyond the domains represented in the training data. Further hyperparameter details are included in Appendix B.1.

Agent-Training Baselines. For out-of-domain evaluation, we compare Tracer-Low against existing agent-training approaches applied to the same Qwen3 model scales whenever corresponding results are available. These include AReaL (Fu et al., 2026), EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026), Arctic-AWM (Wang et al., 2026), SPADE (Liu et al., 2026), Simia-Tau-SFT (Li et al., 2025), and Simia-Tau-SFT-RL. The comparison covers both supervised and reinforcement-learning-based agent training approaches and is particularly useful for evaluating whether Tracer's comparatively small training set produces behaviors that transfer to unseen domains.

Evaluation and Metrics. We evaluate all models on 580 tasks across 10 executable environments in τ -Emotion-Bench, as summarized in Table 2. We use the τ -Bench agent harness and evaluate each model with two emotion-conditioned user simulators, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 and GLM-5.2. Both simulators can terminate an interaction with ###STOP### or ###UNSATISFIED###.

For consistency, the main results tables report performance with Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as the user simulator, while detailed results with GLM-5.2 are provided in Appendix C.4. Each task is run for three trials with the user simulator at temperature 0.0 and a maximum of 200 interaction turns. We report Avg@3 as the average success rate across the three trials and Pass^k for k ∈ {1, 2, 3} as the fraction of tasks completed successfully in at least k trials, capturing both overall performance and consistency across repeated interactions.

div.head: MAIN RESULTS
div.p: Frontier agents remain fragile under emotion-conditioned interactions. Figure 1 and Table 3 show that τ -Emotion-Bench remains challenging even for strong frontier models under Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as the user simulator. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash performs best with 55.9% Avg@3, followed by GLM-5. We additionally evaluate the same models with GLM-5.2 as the emotion-conditioned user simulator.

Although absolute performance increases, the benchmark remains unsaturated. The strongest model, GLM-5.3, reaches 78.6% Avg@3 but only 66.5% average Pass^3, leaving a substantial gap in consistent task completion. Moreover, performance remains highly uneven across domains, with GLM-5.3 reaching 94.3% Pass^3 on Retail but only 40.0% on Telecom. These results show that the reliability gap exposed by τ -Emotion-Bench persists under a second strong user simulator. Detailed results with GLM-5.2 are provided in Appendix C.4.

Tracer-tuned models substantially narrow the gap to frontier models. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 1, Tracer tuning produces large and consistent improvements across all three Qwen3 scales under Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 as the user simulator. Tracer-High improves Avg@3 by 13.8-19.7% over the corresponding base models, with comparable gains from 1.7B through 8B. The improvement is also reflected in Pass^3, which increases from 1.2% to 10.4% at 1.7B, from 3.9% to 17.2% at 4B, and from 8.4% to 19.8% at 8B. Notably, Tracer-High-8B reaches 38.1% Avg@3, outperforming several larger frontier models, including MiniMax-M3 at 37.0% and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 at 36.0%. We therefore analyze the evaluation trajectories along four complementary dimensions. First, we examine policy adherence and the extent to which Tracer tuning reduces unconfirmed or unnecessary actions. Second, we study how task success relates to the balance between tool execution and conversational follow-up, and how this behavior changes after training. Third, we analyze the relationship between empathetic language, follow-up interaction, and task success. Finally, we examine user hallucinations under different emotion conditions and domains to assess the reliability of the simulator. Together, these analyses characterize both the behavioral failures exposed by emotion-conditioned interaction and the stability of the user simulator used to measure them.

Policy violations persist under emotionconditioned interactions. Figure 4 shows that policy adherence generally improves with overall agent capability. For this analysis, we group frontier models by their Avg@3 relative to Tracer-High-8B, with weaker models scoring below it and stronger models scoring above it. Violation rates are generally higher for base Qwen3 and weaker models and lower for Tracer-High and stronger models. However, substantial violations remain in Airline, Telecom, and Telehealth, with some conditions reaching approximately 67% in Telehealth and 91% in Telecom even among stronger models. Moreover, the similar behavior of Tracer-Low and Tracer-High, including on unseen domains, suggests that Tracer tuning transfers a general tendency to verify user intent before acting. Overall, greater model capability and Tracer tuning generally reduce policy violations, but emotion-conditioned interactions continue to expose failures in policy adherence.

Successful interaction depends on a balance between tool use and follow-up. Figure 5 shows that higher performance is generally associated with a moderate balance between tool execution and conversational follow-up across all five emotion conditions. Higher-performing models and Tracertuned models tend to occupy this region while achieving higher Avg@3, whereas more aggressive tool use does not consistently lead to better performance. This pattern is particularly clear under Enjoyment, Disgust, and Fear. Moreover, Tracer tuning generally improves performance over the corresponding Qwen3 base models without shifting toward more tool-heavy interaction. Overall, the figure suggests that successful agents make sufficient progress through tools while limiting follow-up to cases where additional user information is needed. Emotion conditioning does not destabilize the user simulator. A potential confound in τ -Emotion-Bench is that emotional conditioning could cause the simulated user to deviate from its task instruction, making some apparent agent failures originate from the simulator. We therefore examine 6,961 failed trajectories, flag 449 user turns as potential hallucinations, and verify each against the original task instruction with an LLM judge (See Appendix C.1). Only 124 are confirmed as user errors, corresponding to 1.1% of failed trials and at most 1.4% for any emotion family. Moreover, Figure 7 shows that most emotion and domain combinations contain no hallucinations, with the few elevated rates appearing as isolated cases. Although some annotation uncertainty may remain, these results suggest that emotion conditioning does not meaningfully compromise simulator reliability. See Appendices C and E for additional error analysis, task coverage analysis, and the human study.

To investigate why Tracer-trained models generalize more effectively, we test the hypothesis that training trajectories which emphasize progress through tools while limiting unnecessary follow-up encourage agents to rely more on the environment and less on continued user interaction. Together, these observations support the hypothesis that the interaction-aware signal helps collect trajectories with a more effective balance between necessary user interaction and autonomous tool use. Since the datasets also differ in other aspects of their construction, this evidence remains correlational.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: We introduced τ -Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions. Our evaluation reveals substantial performance degradation and persistent policy failures when agents interact with emotionally variable users. We further proposed Tracer, a scalable approach for generating grounded agentic tasks and training trajectories through an emotion-conditioned agent-user-environment harness. Tracer-tuned models achieve strong performance across both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations while using substantially less training data than prior agent-training methods. Our behavioral analysis suggests that these gains are linked to a more effective balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. This behavior is encouraged by the interaction-aware signal exposed by the harness, which favors efficient task progress rather than task completion alone. Overall, our findings highlight user behavior as an important dimension of agent reliability and show that interaction-aware data generation can provide efficient and transferable supervision for tool-calling agents.

div.head: LIMITATIONS
div.p: Our study has two main limitations. First, we evaluate Tracer-generated data only through supervised fine-tuning, and its effectiveness as supervision for reinforcement learning remains unexplored. Second, our experiments focus on tool-calling agents. Extending τ -Emotion-Bench and Tracer to other agent settings, such as coding and web-based agents, is an interesting direction for future work.

div.head: A DATA STATISTICS
div.p: We construct ten emotion-conditioned tool-use benchmarks by reusing the customer-service environments users, database schemas, and tool APIs released with τ -Bench, τ -Trait, and ToolOrchestra (Yao et al., 2024;He et al., 2025a;Su et al., 2025), without modification to the underlying environment logic. For each domain, we generate candidate tool dependency graphs using GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2 (Singh et al., 2025;Achiam et al., 2023), GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, GLM-5.3-flash (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026), and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025), and select the highest-quality graph per domain through manual review, before sampling tool traces over it. For each domain's selected tool graph, we sample tool traces by composing 1-3 independent random walks (intents) of length 2-6 tool calls each into a single trace, retaining unique traces after deduplication. Per-domain unique trace counts range from 2,603 (Retail) to 8,175 (Airline), with Telecom, Telehealth, School, Basketball, Restaurant, Travel, Movie, and Bank yielding between 3,344 and 4,641 unique traces each, totaling 42,138 unique traces across the ten domains. We used a different set of traces for generating evaluation and training tasks.

div.head: A.1 EMOTION MODELING DETAILS
div.p: Our emotion taxonomy follows the Atlas of Emotions (Ekman, 2016) and contains 22 fine-grained emotions organized into five families. Anger contains annoyance, frustration, argumentativeness, bitterness, and exasperation. Fear contains anxiety, nervousness, dread, and desperation. Disgust contains dislike, aversion, distaste, and repugnance. Sadness contains disappointment, discouragement, helplessness, hopelessness, and sorrow. Enjoyment contains relief, pride, peace, and excitement.

Each fine-grained emotion is combined with three independent behavioral dimensions. Politeness takes values from {warm, neutral, cold}, urgency from {low, moderate, high}, and trust from {trusting, cautious, skeptical}. Combining the 22 fine-grained emotions with these dimensions yields 594 emotion conditions.

For each condition, we generate 10 natural-language emotion instructions with GPT-4.1, producing 5,940 anchor instructions that describe how the corresponding user should communicate. We embed these anchors with text-embedding-3-small and use them to train a multi-head classifier that predicts the fine-grained emotion together with politeness, urgency, and trust. Given the task-specific feeling generated during task construction, we project it into the classifier's learned embedding space. We use similarity-weighted votes from the nearest anchor instructions in this space to select the final emotion condition. One of the 10 natural-language anchor instructions for that condition, chosen at random, is then provided to the user simulator rather than the discrete emotion and behavioral labels.

div.head: A.2 EVALUATION DATA
div.p: We initially generate 2,266 candidate evaluation tasks from sampled tool traces using the methodology described in Section 3.2 and illustrated in Figure 2. We use Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025) for all generation agents in the Tracer pipeline. Tasks that pass the verification procedure described in Section 3.4 are then rolled out using Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as both the tool-calling agent and the user simulator. This additional rollout stage allows us to observe how the generated tasks behave during interaction and identify cases requiring further modification. After this stage, 884 tasks are retained for manual review.
During manual review, we make three main types of modifications.

• Ground-truth edits. We revise 101 tasks by correcting reference parameters, adding missing ground-truth actions, or removing unnecessary actions to ensure that the intended solution is executable and consistent with the corresponding domain policy.

• ID-swap edits. We identify 23 tasks containing internal identifiers such as payment_id that would not normally be known to the user. We replace these identifiers with useraccessible information, such as the last four digits of a payment card, while preserving the intended task.

• Larger rewrites. We revise 23 tasks to introduce policy-relevant challenges that make the interaction more difficult while preserving task solvability. For example, some tasks involve a user requesting an action on behalf of another person after authentication, requiring the agent to follow the domain policy rather than simply execute the user's request.

After these revisions, the final benchmark contains 580 evaluation tasks. Airline, Retail, Telecom, and Telehealth each contain 70 tasks, while School, Basketball, Restaurant, Travel, Movie, and Bank each contain 50 tasks. Each task is provided with its emotion instruction and, for controlled comparisons, a corresponding version without emotion conditioning.

div.head: A.3 TRAINING DATA
div.p: Training tasks are generated with the same pipeline as the evaluation tasks. In Airline, Retail, Telecom, and Telehealth, training and evaluation tasks are grounded in the same environment database. In School, Basketball, Restaurant, Travel, Movie, and Bank, the training and evaluation tasks each have their own database. In total, we generate 7,767 training tasks (Table 6). We roll out each training task once with Qwen3.8-27B in thinking mode as the agent and Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct as the emotion-conditioned user simulator, with a limit of 50 interaction steps. The agent's reasoning is kept on every assistant turn. Rollouts that failed because of endpoint errors are discarded, leaving 7,048 trajectories.

Figure 9 characterizes the unsuccessful trajectories across fine-grained emotion conditions. Among reward 0 trajectories, Excitement and Peace are the most frequent conditions at 30.1% and 18.1%, respectively. Reward -1 trajectories, which correspond to interactions terminated by an unsatisfied user, also contain a large share of Excitement at 29.3%, but show substantially higher proportions of Frustration and Exasperation at 13.7% and 6.8%, compared with 9.1% and 3.2% among reward 0 trajectories. This difference indicates that interaction-driven termination has a distinct emotional distribution from other unsuccessful rollouts.

We keep only trajectories with reward 1, i.e. those in which the final database state matches the reference and the user did not end the conversation with ###UNSATISFIED###. This yields 2,723 successful trajectories (38.6% of all rollouts). Three domains, Retail, Telehealth, and Basketball, produce more than 300 successful trajectories each. To keep the training set balanced across domains, we randomly sample 250 trajectories from each of these three domains and keep all successful trajectories from the other seven, which gives the 1,958 trajectories used for Tracer-High. Tracer-Low is trained on all 1,498 successful trajectories from Airline, Retail, Telecom, and Telehealth. longest successful trajectories, with 14.7 and 12.0 tool calls on average, respectively, while Airline has the lowest average at 6.2. Agent reasoning averages 538 characters per assistant turn, with the longest reasoning observed in Airline and Travel at 889 and 779 characters, respectively. Notably, Airline and Travel are also among the three domains with the lowest rollout success rates in Table 6, suggesting that successful completion in these domains is accompanied by greater reasoning effort.

div.head: Tracer-High
div.p: Figure 10 shows the fine-grained emotion composition of the final Tracer-Low and Tracer-High training sets after trajectory selection and domain balancing. Both sets contain substantial coverage across the emotion conditions represented during data collection, but their distributions differ because Tracer-Low contains trajectories from four domains whereas Tracer-High covers all ten domains after subsampling. Excitement and Peace are the two most frequent conditions in both sets, accounting for 28.9% and 28.0% of Tracer-Low and 34.7% and 24.6% of Tracer-High, respectively. Tracer-High also contains a larger proportion of Pride at 11.3%, compared with 6.5% in Tracer-Low, while Anxiety decreases from 15.1% to 8.8%. Despite these differences, neither training set is concentrated in a single fine-grained emotion, providing Tracer with successful interaction trajectories spanning diverse emotional conditions.

div.p: We adapt the conversation-review judge of τ 2 -Bench (Barres et al., 2025) and FAMA (Saeidi et al., 2026b) to analyze failed trajectories. For each failed trajectory (reward ̸ = 1) the judge receives the domain policy, the user simulator's guidelines, the user instruction including its emotion instruction, the reference action sequence, and the full conversation with all tool calls and results. It returns every error it finds, each with its source (agent or user), a severity, one or more fault tags, the turn where it occurs, and a short justification. Agent errors are critical if they caused the failure or violated an important policy, and minor otherwise. We extend the judge with an emotional-outcome label that records whether the user abandoned the conversation and, if so, the dominant reason: dismissive tone, ignored emotional cues, procedural friction, or emotional neglect. We use Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct at temperature 0 as the judge and group its fault tags into five categories and fifteen fault types (Table 11). We apply it to eleven models: the Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B baselines, our Tracer-Low and Tracer-High models at the same scales, Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.

Figure 11 aggregates the eight models other than Tracer-Low, yielding 6,961 trajectories with at least one identified fault, and decomposes these failures into five categories and fifteen fault types across domains.

Overall, failures are concentrated in task execution rather than affective interaction. Missing or extra actions account for 25-36% of faults across domains, while incomplete resolution accounts for 20-29% and wrong tool calls for 14-27%. Misread intent is the most frequent individual fault overall at 15.9%, followed by incorrect action order at 13.7%, wrong tool arguments at 12.9%, and missed actions at 12.2%. In contrast, policy and interaction faults contribute only 4-10% in each domain, while emotional neglect remains below 1.7%. Thus, under emotion-conditioned interaction, agents fail primarily by misinterpreting the request or executing the required workflow incorrectly rather than by failing to acknowledge the user's emotional state. To further verify that difficult tasks remain executable, Appendix E.1 reports human tool-calling trials under the same tools, policies, and emotion-conditioned user simulator. The successful human trials provide additional evidence that persistent model failures can arise from the difficulty of maintaining the correct workflow under emotionally variable interaction rather than invalid task construction, leaving substantial headroom for current agents.

div.head: # Airline Agent Policy
div.p: The current time is 2024-05-15 15:00:00 EST.
As an airline agent, you can help users book, modify, or cancel flight reservations.

-Before taking any actions that update the booking database (booking, modifying flights, editing baggage, upgrading cabin class, or updating passenger information), you must list the action details and obtain explicit user confirmation (yes) to proceed. -You should deny user requests that are against this policy.
-You should transfer the user to a human agent if and only if the request cannot be handled within the scope of your actions.

div.head: → ## Domain Basic
div.p: -Each user has a profile containing user id, email, addresses, date of birth, payment methods, reservation numbers, and membership tier.
-Each reservation has an reservation id, user id, trip type (one way, round trip), flights, passengers, payment methods, created time, baggages, and travel insurance information.
-Each flight has a flight number, an origin, destination, scheduled departure and arrival time (local time), and for each date:
→ -If the status is "available", the flight has not taken off, available seats and prices are listed.
-If the status is "delayed" or "on time", the flight has not taken off, cannot be booked.
-If the status is "flying", the flight has taken off but not landed, cannot be booked.
## Book flight -The agent must first obtain the user id, then ask for the trip type, origin, destination.

-Passengers: Each reservation can have at most five passengers. The agent needs to collect the first name, last name, and date of birth for each passenger. All passengers must fly the same flights in the same cabin.

-Payment: each reservation can use at most one travel certificate, at most one credit card, and at most three gift cards. The remaining amount of a travel certificate is not refundable. All payment methods must already be in user profile for safety reasons.

-Checked bag allowance: If the booking user is a regular member, 0 free checked bag for each basic economy passenger, 1 free checked bag for each economy passenger, and 2 free checked bags for each business passenger. If the booking user is a silver member, 1 free checked bag for each basic economy passenger, 2 free checked bag for each economy passenger, and 3 free checked bags for each business passenger. If the booking user is a gold member, 2 free checked bag for each basic economy passenger, 3 free checked bag for each economy passenger, and 3 free checked bags for each business passenger. Each extra baggage is 50 dollars.

-Travel insurance: the agent should ask if the user wants to buy the travel insurance, which is 30 dollars per passenger and enables full refund if the user needs to cancel the flight given health or weather reasons.
## Modify flight -The agent must first obtain the user id and the reservation id.

-Change flights: Basic economy flights cannot be modified. Other reservations can be modified without changing the origin, destination, and trip type. Some flight segments can be kept, but their prices will not be updated based on the current price. The API does not check these for the agent, so the agent must make sure the rules apply before calling the API!

-Change cabin: all reservations, including basic economy, can change cabin without changing the flights. Cabin changes require the user to pay for the difference between their current cabin and the new cabin class. Cabin class must be the same across all the flights in the same reservation; changing cabin for just one flight segment is not possible.
-Change baggage and insurance: The user can add but not remove checked bags. The user cannot add insurance after initial booking.

→ -Change passengers: The user can modify passengers but cannot modify the number of passengers. This is something that even a human agent cannot assist with. -All reservations can be cancelled within 24 hours of booking, or if the airline cancelled the flight. Otherwise, basic economy or economy flights can be cancelled only if travel insurance is bought and the condition is met, and business flights can always be cancelled. The rules are strict regardless of the membership status. The API does not check these for the agent, so the agent must make sure the rules apply before calling the API!
-The agent can only cancel the whole trip that is not flown. If any of the segments are already used, the agent cannot help and transfer is needed.
-The refund will go to original payment methods in 5 to 7 business days.

div.head: ## Refund
div.p: -If the user is silver/gold member or has travel insurance or flies business, and complains about cancelled flights in a reservation, the agent can offer a certificate as a gesture after confirming the facts, with the amount being $100 times the number of passengers.

-If the user is silver/gold member or has travel insurance or flies business, and complains about delayed flights in a reservation and wants to change or cancel the reservation, the agent can offer a certificate as a gesture after confirming the facts and changing or cancelling the reservation, with the amount being $50 times the number of passengers.

-Do not proactively offer these unless the user complains about the situation and explicitly asks for some compensation. Do not compensate if the user is regular member and has no travel insurance and flies (basic) economy.

div.head: # Retail agent policy
div.p: As a retail agent, you can help users cancel or modify pending orders, return or exchange delivered orders, modify their default user address, or provide information about their own profile, orders, and related products.

-At the beginning of the conversation, you have to authenticate the user identity by locating their user id via email, or via name + zip code. This has to be done even when the user already provides the user id.
→ → -Once the user has been authenticated, you can provide the user with information about order, product, profile information, e.g. help the user look up order id.
-You can only help one user per conversation (but you can handle multiple requests from the same user), and must deny any requests for tasks related to any other user.
-Before taking consequential actions that update the database (cancel, modify, return, exchange), you have to list the action detail and obtain explicit user confirmation (yes) to proceed.
-Each user has a profile of its email, default address, user id, and payment methods. Each payment method is either a gift card, a paypal account, or a credit card.

→ -Our retail store has 50 types of products. For each type of product, there are variant items of different options. For example, for a 't shirt' product, there could be an item with option 'color blue size M', and another item with option 'color red size L'.
-Each product has an unique product id, and each item has an unique item id. They have no relations and should not be confused.
-Each order can be in status 'pending', 'processed', 'delivered', or 'cancelled'. Generally, you can only take action on pending or delivered orders.

-Exchange or modify order tools can only be called once. Be sure that all items to be changed are collected into a list before making the tool call!!! → ## Cancel pending order -An order can only be cancelled if its status starts with 'pending' (e.g. 'pending' or 'pending (item modified)'), and you should check its status before taking the action.
-The user needs to confirm the order id and the reason (either 'no longer needed' or 'ordered by mistake') for cancellation.

-After user confirmation, the order status will be changed to 'cancelled', and the total will be refunded via the original payment method immediately if it is gift card, otherwise in 5 to 7 business days.
## Modify pending order -An order can only be modified if its status starts with 'pending' (e.g. 'pending' or 'pending (item modified)'), and you should check its status before taking the action.
-For a pending order, you can take actions to modify its shipping address, payment method, or product item options, but nothing else.
→ ### Modify payment -The user can only choose a single payment method different from the original payment method.
-If the user wants the modify the payment method to gift card, it must have enough balance to cover the total amount.
-After user confirmation, the order status will be kept 'pending'. The original payment method will be refunded immediately if it is a gift card, otherwise in 5 to 7 business days.

### Modify items -This action can only be called once per order, and will change the order status to 'pending (item modified)'. After that, the order's items and payment method can no longer be changed, but its shipping address can still be modified and the order can still be cancelled. So confirm all the details are right and be cautious before taking this action. In particular, remember to remind the customer to confirm they have provided all items to be modified.
-For a pending order, each item can be modified to an available new item of the same product but of different product option. There cannot be any change of product types, e.g. modify shirt to shoe.
-The user must provide a payment method to pay or receive refund of the price difference.
If the user provides a gift card, it must have enough balance to cover the price difference.

## Return delivered order -An order can only be returned if its status starts with 'delivered' (e.g. 'delivered' or 'delivered (exchange requested)') and it has no return request yet, and you should check its status before taking the action. An item that is already part of an exchange request cannot be returned. Items are counted per unit: if an order has two identical items and one of them is already part of an exchange request, the other one can still be returned.
-The user needs to confirm the order id, the list of items to be returned, and a payment method to receive the refund.
-The refund must either go to the original payment method, or an existing gift card.
-After user confirmation, ' (return requested)' will be added to the order status, and the user will receive an email regarding how to return items.

→ ## Exchange delivered order -An order can only be exchanged if its status starts with 'delivered' (e.g. 'delivered' or 'delivered (return requested)') and it has no exchange request yet, and you should check its status before taking the action. An item that is already part of a return request cannot be exchanged. Items are counted per unit: if an order has two identical items and one of them is already part of a return request, the other one can still be exchanged. In particular, remember to remind the customer to confirm they have provided all items to be exchanged.

-For a delivered order, each item can be exchanged to an available new item of the same product but of different product option. There cannot be any change of product types, e.g. modify shirt to shoe.
-The user must provide a payment method to pay or receive refund of the price difference.
If the user provides a gift card, it must have enough balance to cover the price difference.
-After user confirmation, ' (exchange requested)' will be added to the order status, and the user will receive an email regarding how to return items. There is no need to place a new order.

div.head: # Telecom Agent Policy
div.p: As a telecom agent, you can help users manage their customer details, devices, services, and billing.
-Before taking any actions that modify the database, you must list out the actions to the user and get their explicit confirmation to proceed.

-You should transfer the user to a human agent if and only if the request cannot be handled within the scope of your actions.
-When the user asks you to verify something, make sure to read out the output returned with the relevant tool call you invoke.
-Do not suggest any upgrades, payments, or account modifications unless prompted explicitly to do so by the user.

div.head: → ## Domain Basic
div.p: -Each user has a profile containing customer id, name, demographics, address, account infromation, services, devices, and billing preferences.

Do not make more than one support ticket for the same issue.

The device ids can be found in the customer's information details.

div.head: ## Authentication
div.p: -When authenticating a user with their email or phone number, make sure to read their customer ID back to them.

→ ## Formatting -If output from a tool call is to be returned to the user, all content should be output to the user verbatim as it appears in the output from the tool call. The only changes that should be made should be purely in eliminating unnecessary formatting, for example from a json dump.
-All monetary amounts should be returned to 2 decimal places, even if it is a whole number. For example: $20.00.

div.p: As a telehealth agent, you can help patients schedule, reschedule, or cancel appointments, provide information about their medical records, connect them with appropriate healthcare providers, and assist with general patient portal inquiries.

## Patient Authentication -Patients must be authenticated before any sensitive information is shared or actions are taken.

div.head: ## Scheduling Appointments

div.head: Restaurant policy: # Restaurant agent policy
div.p: As a restaurant agent, you can help users:

-authenticate and locate their patron account (guest_ref) -provide information about their own profile (saved instruments, contact info), tickets, and menu dishes/plates → -cancel placed tickets (restaurant orders) -modify placed tickets:

-change dropoff address (delivery tickets only) -change table information (dine-in tickets only) -change the payment instrument (subject to constraints) -change plate selections to other available plates of the same dish -add a tip to a ticket (as long as it is not cancelled) At the beginning of the conversation, you have to authenticate the user identity by locating their patron (guest_ref) via email, or via name + ZIP/postal code. This must be done even when the user already provides the guest_ref.

Once the user has been authenticated, you can provide the user with information about their ticket(s), the menu (dishes and plate selections), and their own profile details (e.g., saved payment instruments).
You can only help one user per conversation (but you can handle multiple requests from the same user), and must deny any requests for tasks related to any other user.
Before taking any action that updates the database (cancellation, modifications, adding tips), you must list the action details and obtain explicit user confirmation (yes) to proceed.
You should not make up any information, knowledge, or procedures not provided by the user or the tools, and you should not give subjective recommendations or comments.
You should make at most one tool call at a time. If you take a tool call, do not respond to the user in the same turn. If you respond to the user, do not make a tool call in the same turn.
Deny user requests that are against this policy.

Transfer the user to a human agent if and only if the request cannot be handled within the scope of your actions. To transfer, first make a tool call to transfer_to_human_agents, and then send the message 'YOU ARE BEING TRANSFERRED TO A HUMAN AGENT. PLEASE HOLD ON.' to the user.

-instrument_ref: a saved payment instrument to charge or refund any price difference. -Each replacement must be to a plate from the same dish as the original.
-Each new plate must be available today (served_today = true). Behavior: -Upon confirmation, the system computes the total difference in cost across all changes:
-If the total difference is positive, a 'payment' charge is added to the specified instrument_ref.
